zh.q: 食盐、氨和 CO₂ 进去，纯碱怎么出来的？
zh.concl: 盐 + 氨 + CO₂ 在溶液里生成 NaHCO₃ 析出，煅烧得纯碱；母液加盐降温还捞出 NH₄Cl——侯氏法因此革除了氨碱法的石灰窑与蒸氨塔。
points: 前段：化盐 + 吸氨 + 碳化，生成 NaHCO₃ 并析出；后段：过滤、煅烧得纯碱，母液再捞 NH₄Cl。
五个工段各解决一个问题：通气顺序、过饱和析出、固液分离、受热分解、母液与 CO₂ 回收。
侯氏法比氨碱法少了石灰窑与蒸氨塔，副产可作氮肥的 NH₄Cl，食盐利用率大大提高。

zh.q: 为什么非要先把盐水变成氨盐水？
zh.concl: NH₃ 让溶液显碱性，CO₂ 才被大量吸收、以 HCO₃⁻ 存在；没有氨，过饱和度上不去，几乎什么都析不出来。
points: NH₃ 极易溶于水，氨水显碱性，CO₂ 被大量吸收并以 HCO₃⁻ 的形式存在。
先通 CO₂ 则溶液偏酸，HCO₃⁻ 远远不够，大量 CO₂ 随尾气跑掉。
本课只演示「吸氨中断」这一种情形（模型没有气体累计量与顺序状态），不与「先通 CO₂、后补 NH₃」混为一谈。

zh.q: 生成的 NaHCO₃ 为什么会自己从溶液里掉出来？
zh.concl: 20 ℃ 时 NaHCO₃ 的溶解度 9.6 g/100 g 水是四种里最小的；在氨盐水中它又很快达到过饱和——过饱和才是析出的判据，溶解度排序只作定性参考。
points: 20 ℃ 时 NaHCO₃ 的溶解度 9.6 g/100 g 水，是四种物质里最小的（NH₄HCO₃ 21.7、NaCl 35.9、NH₄Cl 37.2）。
真正决定析出的是过饱和：氨盐水里生成的 NaHCO₃ 超过了它的溶解度上限，才以晶体形式出来。
「溶解度最小」只说明它最容易先走到那一步，是定性参考，不是充分条件。
不做这一步：学生会把「溶解度排序 = 析出判据」当成结论——旧版这条主线改了 5 轮，就是为它。

zh.q: 既然温度越低越容易析出，为什么工业上还要控在 25~40 ℃？
zh.concl: 升温溶解度变大、过饱和变小，析出率单调下降；但温度太低动力学跟不上（10 ℃ 只有 15.95 t/h），所以工业取 25~40 ℃ 并冷却控温。
points: 温度越高、过饱和度越小，析出率从 32.6 % 单调降到 21.1 %。
温度太低反应又太慢（10 ℃ 只有 15.95 t/h），所以工业把碳化控在 25~40 ℃ 并冷却移热。
不控温：塔内一路升到 55 ℃，产量只剩 13.81 t/h（约额定的 58 %）。

zh.q: 塔底出来的晶浆，怎么变成两种东西？
zh.concl: 过滤把重碱（去煅烧）与母液（去冷析结晶器）分开；母液处理后循环回氨化，这一步不改变析出量。
points: 碳化塔底出来的是晶浆：NaHCO₃ 晶体悬浮在母液里。
转鼓真空过滤把固体（重碱）与液体（母液）分开，这一步不改变平衡、也不改变析出量。
两路各有去处：重碱去煅烧，母液去冷析结晶器捞 NH₄Cl，剩下的母液循环回氨化。

zh.q: 重碱要烧到什么程度才是纯碱？
zh.concl: 2NaHCO₃ ─△→ Na₂CO₃ + CO₂↑ + H₂O，160 ℃ 以上才分解完全；温度太低产品里还是小苏打，太高（> 320 ℃）会熔结停车。
points: 煅烧让 NaHCO₃ 分解：2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂↑，放出的 CO₂ 回收再用。
工业区间 160~230 ℃；本课模型里 100 ℃ 分解率为 0、160 ℃ 起 100 %（分段规则，不是实测界限）。
温度不够，产品里还是小苏打，产量只有 8.00 t/h（分解率 33.3 %）；温度过高（> 320 ℃）会熔结停车。

zh.q: 母液里剩下的东西，怎么变成氮肥？
zh.concl: 母液加 NaCl 到饱和（同离子效应）再降到 10 ℃ 以下，NH₄Cl 才过饱和析出、做成氮肥；煅烧回收的 CO₂ 与合成氨副产一起供碳化——这就是「联合」。
points: 母液里还剩下 NH₄Cl：加 NaCl 到饱和（同离子效应）再降到 10 ℃ 以下，它才过饱和结晶出来。
析出的 NH₄Cl 是氮肥；煅烧回收的 CO₂ 与合成氨副产一起供碳化，供给覆盖率 62 %，关掉回收只剩 30 %。
不回收母液：NH₄Cl 随废液排掉，既浪费氮又污染水体——这正是侯氏法比氨碱法多出来的那笔收益。

zh.q: 你来当班长：能不能让这一班稳稳达产？
zh.concl: 达产 = 每一段都守在区间里：顺序对了、温度对了、分解完全、母液和 CO₂ 都循环起来。
points: 达标要五段同时守住：吸氨开、碳化 25~40 ℃、煅烧 160~230 ℃、冷析 ≤ 15 ℃（本课放宽到 15 ℃ 便于操作，设定）、循环开。
产量 = 析出率 × 碳化程度 × 循环 × 分解率，任何一项塌下来产量就掉一个台阶。
中途会出一次碳化温度偏高的异常，要自己拉回来，别让它拖过 15 s。
达产不是某一个旋钮的事：只调一个滑块拿不到 22 t/h。

en.q: Salt, ammonia and CO₂ go in: how does soda ash come out?
en.concl: Salt + ammonia + CO₂ form NaHCO₃ in solution, which precipitates and is calcined to soda ash; adding salt to the mother liquor and cooling also recovers NH₄Cl, which is how Hou's process eliminated the lime kiln and ammonia still of the ammonia-soda process.
points: Front end: dissolve salt + absorb ammonia + carbonate, forming and precipitating NaHCO₃; back end: filter and calcine for soda ash, then recover NH₄Cl from the mother liquor.
Each of the five sections solves one problem: gas order, supersaturated precipitation, solid–liquid separation, thermal decomposition, recovery of mother liquor and CO₂.
Compared with the ammonia-soda (Solvay) process, Hou's process drops the lime kiln and ammonia still, yields NH₄Cl usable as nitrogen fertilizer, and greatly improves salt utilization.

en.q: Why must the brine be turned into ammoniated brine first?
en.concl: NH₃ makes the solution basic so CO₂ is absorbed in large amounts as HCO₃⁻; without ammonia the supersaturation can't build and almost nothing precipitates.
points: NH₃ is very soluble in water and ammonia water is basic, so CO₂ is absorbed in large amounts and exists as HCO₃⁻.
With CO₂ first the solution is acidic, HCO₃⁻ falls far short, and a lot of CO₂ escapes with the tail gas.
This lesson only demonstrates "ammonia absorption interrupted" (the model has no cumulative gas amounts or order state), which isn't the same as "CO₂ first, NH₃ added later".

en.q: Why does the NaHCO₃ formed drop out of solution on its own?
en.concl: At 20 ℃ NaHCO₃'s solubility of 9.6 g/100 g water is the lowest of the four, and in ammoniated brine it quickly becomes supersaturated; supersaturation is the criterion for precipitation, and the solubility ranking is only a qualitative guide.
points: At 20 ℃ the solubility of NaHCO₃ is 9.6 g/100 g water, the lowest of the four substances (NH₄HCO₃ 21.7, NaCl 35.9, NH₄Cl 37.2).
What really decides precipitation is supersaturation: the NaHCO₃ formed in the ammoniated brine exceeds its solubility limit and comes out as crystals.
"Lowest solubility" only means it gets there first; it's a qualitative guide, not a sufficient condition.
Skip this step and students conclude "solubility ranking = precipitation criterion"; the old version of this main thread was revised five times for exactly this.

en.q: If lower temperatures precipitate more easily, why does industry keep it at 25–40 ℃?
en.concl: Raising the temperature increases solubility and lowers supersaturation, so the precipitation rate falls steadily; but too low a temperature slows the kinetics (only 15.95 t/h at 10 ℃), so industry uses 25–40 ℃ with cooling control.
points: NaHCO₃ solubility rises with temperature: 8.1 at 10 ℃, 11.1 at 30 ℃, 13.5 g/100 g water at 45 ℃.
The higher the temperature, the lower the supersaturation, and the precipitation rate falls steadily from 32.6 % to 21.1 %.
Too low a temperature makes the reaction too slow (only 15.95 t/h at 10 ℃), so industry keeps carbonation at 25–40 ℃ with cooling to remove heat.
Without temperature control the tower climbs to 55 ℃ and output falls to 13.81 t/h (about 58 % of rated).

en.q: How does the slurry from the bottom of the tower become two things?
en.concl: Filtration separates crude bicarbonate (to calcination) from mother liquor (to the cooling crystallizer); after treatment the liquor is recycled to ammoniation, and this step doesn't change the amount precipitated.
points: What comes out of the bottom of the carbonation tower is slurry: NaHCO₃ crystals suspended in mother liquor.
The rotary vacuum filter separates the solid (crude bicarbonate) from the liquid (mother liquor); this step changes neither the equilibrium nor the amount precipitated.
Each stream has its destination: crude bicarbonate to calcination, mother liquor to the cooling crystallizer to recover NH₄Cl, with the remaining liquor recycled to ammoniation.

en.q: How far must crude bicarbonate be heated to become soda ash?
en.concl: 2NaHCO₃ ─△→ Na₂CO₃ + CO₂↑ + H₂O, complete only above 160 ℃; too cold and the product is still baking soda, too hot (> 320 ℃) and it sinters and shuts down.
points: Calcination decomposes NaHCO₃: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂↑, and the CO₂ released is recovered and reused.
The industrial range is 160–230 ℃; in this lesson's model decomposition is 0 at 100 ℃ and 100 % from 160 ℃ (a piecewise rule, not a measured boundary).
Not hot enough and the product is still baking soda, with output only 8.00 t/h (decomposition 33.3 %); too hot (> 320 ℃) and it sinters and the plant shuts down.

en.q: How does what's left in the mother liquor become nitrogen fertilizer?
en.concl: Add NaCl to the mother liquor to saturation (common-ion effect) and cool below 10 ℃, and NH₄Cl supersaturates and precipitates as nitrogen fertilizer; CO₂ recovered from calcination joins ammonia-synthesis by-product to feed carbonation: that's the "combined" part.
points: NH₄Cl remains in the mother liquor: add NaCl to saturation (common-ion effect) and cool below 10 ℃, and only then does it supersaturate and crystallize.
The lower the cooling temperature, the higher the crystallization rate: 15.4 % at 30 ℃, 30.0 % at 20 ℃, 44.0 % at 10 ℃.

The NH₄Cl that precipitates is a nitrogen fertilizer; CO₂ recovered from calcination joins by-product CO₂ from ammonia synthesis to feed carbonation, with 62 % supply coverage, or only 30 % with recovery off.
Without recovering the mother liquor, NH₄Cl goes out with the waste liquid, wasting nitrogen and polluting water; that's exactly the extra gain Hou's process has over the ammonia-soda process.

en.q: You're the shift lead: can you get this shift steadily to target output?
en.concl: Hitting target = every section held within its range: correct order, correct temperatures, complete decomposition, and both mother liquor and CO₂ recycled.
points: To pass, all five sections must hold at once: ammonia absorption on, carbonation 25–40 ℃, calcination 160–230 ℃, cooling ≤ 15 ℃ (relaxed to 15 ℃ in this lesson for easier operation, a setting), recycling on.
Output = precipitation rate × carbonation degree × recycling × decomposition rate; if any one collapses, output drops a level.
Partway through there will be one fault with carbonation temperature running high; bring it back yourself and don't let it drag past 15 s.
Hitting target isn't about one knob: adjusting a single slider won't get 22 t/h.
